n: Jesus tells His disciples about a wealthy man whose estate manager was reported for mismanaging and wasting his property.

f.g: A household manager who handled the owner’s business and accounts.
The same word used of the prodigal son “wasting” his substance.

n: The owner calls him in, demands a final accounting, and tells him he is fired.

f.w: give an account of thy stewardship

n: The steward panics. He’s not strong enough for manual labor and too proud to beg. What will he do?

f.g: Digging was hard manual labor for the lowest workers.

n: He comes up with a plan to make friends who will take him in once he loses his job.

f.g: I know what I’ll do.

n: Before word of his firing gets out, he calls in each of his master’s debtors one by one.

f.g: Probably tenant farmers or merchants who owed goods.

n: One owes a hundred measures of olive oil; the steward has him rewrite the bill for fifty — a huge discount.

f.g: About 800–900 gallons — the yield of roughly 150 olive trees.
The written promissory note.

n: Another owes a hundred measures of wheat; the steward reduces it to eighty. Now these men owe him a favor.

f.g: Eighty (four times twenty).
A large quantity — perhaps the harvest of about a hundred acres.

n: The master grudgingly admires his shrewdness — not his dishonesty. Jesus observes that worldly people are often more clever about their futures than God’s people are about eternity.

f.g: Praised — for his foresight, not his ethics.

n: Use worldly wealth to bless others and build eternal friendships, so that when money fails, you will be welcomed into eternal homes. Money is a tool for heavenly purposes.

f.g: An Aramaic word for wealth or possessions, here almost personified as a rival god.

n: How we handle small things shows how we’ll handle big ones. Faithfulness and dishonesty both begin in little matters.

f.w: faithful in that which is least

n: If we can’t be trusted with money, which is temporary, how can God trust us with true, eternal riches?
Everything we have really belongs to God; we are stewards. Faithfulness with what is His prepares us to receive what will eternally be our own.
You can’t be fully devoted to two masters. Ultimately, you must choose: God or money.

f.w: No servant can serve two masters

n: The Pharisees, who loved money, hear this and sneer at Jesus.

f.g: Lovers of money.
Scoffed, literally “turned up their noses.”

n: Jesus replies that they make themselves look righteous to people, but God sees their hearts. What society prizes, God often despises. The JST adds several verses here expanding His reply.

f.g: Something detestable.

n: The law and prophets pointed forward until John the Baptist. Now God’s kingdom is being preached, and people are pushing eagerly to get in.

f.g: Forces their way in — eagerly entering.

n: This doesn’t mean God’s law is discarded. Heaven and earth would vanish sooner than the smallest part of it would fail; Christ came to fulfill it.

f.g: A tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.

f.w: one tittle of the law to fail

n: As an example of the law’s enduring force, Jesus upholds the sacredness of marriage. Divorcing to marry someone else is adultery — a stricter standard than the Pharisees taught.

f.g: Divorces her.

n: Another story: a rich man dresses in royal purple and expensive linen and feasts luxuriously every day.

f.g: Purple dye was very costly; this was the clothing of royalty and the extremely rich.
Lavishly.

n: At his gate lies a beggar named Lazarus, covered in sores. He is the only character in Jesus’ parables given a name — the poor man is known to God.

f.g: A form of Eleazar, “God has helped.”
Placed there by others — he couldn’t walk.

n: He longs for scraps from the rich man’s table. Only street dogs pay him attention, licking his sores.

f.g: Scraps; sometimes bread used to wipe hands was thrown under the table.

n: Both die. Angels carry Lazarus to Abraham’s side — a place of honor and rest. The rich man is simply buried.

f.g: A Jewish image of paradise — reclining next to Abraham at the heavenly feast.

n: In the spirit world the rich man is in torment. He can see Abraham far away with Lazarus beside him.

f.g: Greek hadēs — the spirit world; latter-day scripture calls this part of it spirit prison.

n: Now he begs for mercy — but still treats Lazarus as a servant to be sent on an errand.

f.g: Scripture often describes the anguish of a guilty conscience as fire.

n: Abraham gently reminds him: you had your comforts in life; Lazarus had suffering. Now their situations are reversed.

f.g: Abraham still addresses him kindly.

f.w: thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things

n: A great gulf separates the two places, and no one can cross. Latter-day revelation teaches that Christ, after His death, bridged this gulf by organizing the preaching of the gospel to the spirits in prison.
The rich man then asks Abraham to send Lazarus to his family’s home.

f.g: His family.

n: He has five brothers and wants Lazarus to warn them so they won’t end up in this place of torment.

f.g: Warn them solemnly.

n: Abraham answers that they already have the scriptures — Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to those.

f.g: The Hebrew scriptures, our Old Testament.

n: The rich man insists that a visitor from the dead would surely convince them to repent.
Abraham’s answer is sobering: if they ignore the scriptures, not even a resurrection will persuade them. Soon, Jesus Himself would rise from the dead — and many would still not believe.

f.w: though one rose from the dead
